Hacknet is pretty much what it says on the tin - a hacking-themed game in which you must meet escalating challenges throughout the course of its story, which opens with a posthumous message coming from a hacker who has disappeared.  Stop right there, though - the story isn't very strong on the conspiracy and ends up being a missed opportunity, so don't dive in just yet.

Those not familiar with command-lines need not fret as this isn't a full-blown OS simulator like other games in the genre.  While it does have its own level of CLI sophistication, the tutorial and pacing thereafter is carefully crafted as not to overwhelm the inexperienced.  Anyone looking to roleplay a super hacking machine can comfortably play this game without having a manual in front of them (though a notepad may help).  Rather than have you coding a bunch of exploits or what have you, your hacking terminal - which is beautifully-rendered, btw - is loaded with magical tools that do all the work for you.  You just need to handle the set up, if you will, and the software will do the rest.

What separates Hacknet from others in the genre is its combo of command-line terminal and graphical user interface (think X-Window).  The game is aesthetically pleasing to the eye with a mix of hi- and low-tech, giving the interface an authentic OS feel.  If you're not keen on typing every little thing (which you can absolutely elect to do), you can instead click on the GUI to navigate around most of the systems and poke around.  You'll still need to key in some commands, but there's a good balance here if you want to save some time with navigation and reading files.  Websites aren't functional, but they do appear in the game and give it that extra little flavor, with one exception being a Clicker game that you can waste time on should you so choose to.

So while the story doesn't really play out in the best of ways, the hacking is quite fun... at least for the first little bit.  It very soon becomes repetitive because ultimately the puzzles are limited.  You will be taking on contracts/jobs from message servers and they each boil down to a) get into the target system and b) grab some information or delete stuff.  Even though you are introduced to new tools (and thus, the difficulty of breaking into a system increases), the game rarely deviates from this formula, even when the story demands it.  It's not really until the latter quarter of the game when you're doing interesting stuff, not so much because the repetitiveness is gone, but more because the answers aren't quite as obvious.

I would have liked to have a more involved tale form throughout the game and as I said above, it's a missed opportunity.  It would make discovery so much more satisfying.  This isn't made much better by most servers being devoid of anything interesting other than some randomly-pulled bash quotes which, if you've been around on the Internet long enough, you've already read.  Still, this is a minor nitpick and beyond that, there was nary an issue with the game.  I encountered no bugs or crashes, except that I wasted a good 2 or 3 hours trying to go down a different path (which happens under very, very specific circumstances), which highlighted the inability to save-where-you-want; basically, failing to meet the conditions, even though I thought I knew what I had to do, meant that I had to restart from scratch repeatedly just to get there... however, this alternate path is completely optional and easily-missed.  I only put this here as a warning to achievement hunters.

At the end of the day, Hacknet is a fun game that captures the spirit of hacking without overwhelming the player.  I'm sure there are more hardcore games in the genre, but at that point - in my opinion - I feel it stops being a game and starts being a job.  Hacknet manages to find the right balance between authenticity and Hollywood fantasy so it's a very enjoyable experience.

Just be aware that the blue screens look incredibly authentic.  Don't panic.

* Hacks into it, removes some file.
* Suddenly gets attacked with an email worm
* loses a desktop, has to continue using command prompt only
* goes back to proxy, cracks it again.
* Downloads the proxy's desktop environment from his server.
* Finds the email worm that was send to me, downloads it.
* Reboots PC, has a desktop again.

I hoped this game would be a spiritual successor to Uplink maybe with a little bit more realism. Unfortunately the game falls short of that aspiration.

First of all, it's not any more realistic than Uplink. While you get to use real Unix commands, you don't use them in a very similar way to the real thing. Have no illusion, this game will not teach you anything useful in real life. There's nothing wrong with making your hacking sim game a little over the top with fancy animations and misused tech lingo, but it's not what I expected.

Where the game really fails to live up to Uplink, however, is depth. Remember how Uplink had news bulletins reporting on your mischief, other active hackers taking assignments and getting arrested when you rat on them, multiple banks with multiple accounts wiring funds to each other, and a stock market where you could watch your victim corporations suffer losses after you hack and destroy their mainframes? You will find nothing like this in Hacknet. All you get it a lot of random IRC logs pasted from bash.org and some personal files and emails that are not written in a breathtaking way.

Is it fun? Yeah, especially if it's your first game of this kind. There's a thrill in accessing systems and files you shouldn't be looking at and there's even an overarching plot that's encouraging you to keep playing, but it all lacks depth, gameplay-wise, story-wise and writing-wise.

This was my first hacking style game, and I'm very impressed with how Hacknet was made. It has a certain charm to it, a great story (I haven't tried the new Labyrinths dlc yet), but I've heard amazing things about it as well. It uses real Linux/ Unix commands, so you could learn a few things along with the adventure and mystery you already get. In my opinion, even if some people don't like games unless they have movie-style cinematics, or "amazing graphics", they might like this game if they gave it a try, instead of watching a hacker, you could be one. Childhood dream realized in an amazingly made game. Don't change the art you guys have created Team Fractal Alligator. :D

I love, love, LOVE this game.

If you have any exposure to webdev, networking, programming, or just find yourself using the terminal often, you owe it to yourself to try this experience.

The mechanics are simple enough for a novice to begin with, but quickly ramp up. This is a game that requires critical thinking, good knowledge retention, and the ability to quickly develop new skills.

One thing that this game really nails is atmosphere, and that's saying something since there are zero fancy 3D polygons to be found anywhere. You really [i]feel[/i] like a hacker in this game, navigating systems you have no authorization to, extracting data from otherwise closed sources, and constantly being reminded that human behaviour is ultimately the downfall of any good security system.

The DLC is a separate experience that builds on the base game, introducing new mechanics, programs, and hacks. Minor spoiler, but when [spoiler] you are kicked out of the actual "game" and have to interact with your own machine's terminal and a text file as your guide [/spoiler] it is an absolute amazing experience.

I cannot wait to dive into the user-created Workshop content, adding whole new chapters and stories that leverage the games mechanics, and I already have some ideas for my very own Extension.

8.5 / 10 for base game
9 / 10 including the Labyrinths expansion DLC

Terribly disappointed by this game. Even the 3€ something during the most recent sale were too much, imho.

While the Game does use some Linux command line inputs to navigate on the computer (cd to change folders, ls to list contents, cat to read a file), those become useless once you completed the tutorial and gain access to the User Interface (mouse control), which is much faster.
"Hacking" works by starting skripts that automate the whole process. All you have to do is start the same 5 skripts by typing their name:
If there is a proxy active, use your own to overload it (click the overwhelm button).
If there is a firewall active, type analyze 5 times, then type solve and the password that was just revealed.
For any available port, type the name of the corresponding skript, wait for it to finish (about 10 seconds), then start the next one.
Sometimes, there is a time limit that never really got close to bothering me.

The story is either really weak or did not really start by the time I quit. You get a first E-Mail (I don't know you, please help me). Then, to build up your skills, you hack at least two dozen systems, always using the method described above, working your way up in some hacker organization you don't really know anything about. When you finally find that you are done with them, you start at bottom level of the next organization.

Conclusion:
Apart from my desire not to leave the game unfinished, there is absolutely nothing that would make me keep playing. Not recommended.
